marrak_sen.name: Warden Marrak Sen
marrak_sen.personality: weathered, pragmatic, quietly furious at the Queen's tolls
marrak_sen.voice: caravan ledgers and well-depth readings; clipped, with long pauses before bad news

say: Marrak Sen, Warden of Redwater. The well is deep, the shade is cheap, and the tolls are not. You have come from Khesh-Ura with a writ in your pocket, so you know the Queen's road is closed to most.

Three weeks ago a lizardfolk warlord named Vesh-Kar took the old Toll Fort north of here. He stops every caravan and takes a tenth of every cargo, and now it is a tenth of every drop and every grain. We have not had a wagon through in nineteen days.
Go north over the ridge and break his hold. The road beyond is crawling with scorpions and warbands, so take good steel and plenty of potions. I will keep the well open for you.
The fort's banner is down. Through a spyglass on the ridge I saw the banner drop, and I wept into the lens. Nineteen days, and now it is over.
That writ you found. 'One tenth of the sun.' I always thought the Queen was a thief. It is worse. She is a collector, and she does not know where to stop.

Take these supplies and this purse. This brass token opens the east road to Perch, the cliff village, where the old wind-warden has been asking after travellers. Ismerel will hear of this before the week is out.

lines.text: The well at Redwater is three hundred feet deep. The old priests dug it by hand, with a prayer between every bucket.
I keep a ledger of every cart, every camel, every traveller. When the ledger stops growing, I know the road has died.
Vessa sells honest steel. Noor sells honest beds. I sell honest water. Between the three of us, we are the only honest thing in the dunes.
A caravan from the east came through last spring with silks and a dead guard. The guard had no wounds. I did not ask.
The camels are patient animals. They have outlasted two Queens and an unpleasant emperor. Study them.
I do not drink the first cup from a new well. A habit of my father's. He was right more often than he was kind.
A fighter. Good. The fort's spearmen hold a shield wall, and a shield wall needs something to break against.
A mage. Lizardfolk fear the cold. Frost will drop them where fire only makes them yawn.
A scout. The scorpions burrow in the loose sand beyond the second milestone. Walk the stone, not the dune.
A healer. Poison is the road's only sure killer. Bring antidotes. Bring many.
In summer the stones crack at noon like pistol shots. It scares new drovers half to death.
Dilly runs messages to Khesh-Ura on foot. Three days there, three days back, and not a word of complaint. I am considering a medal.
Old Haggar tells stories about the Queen's early days. Half of them are lies. The other half are worse.
Ellis draws maps of the glass dunes. I told him no one will buy them. He drew another one.
A rare trader comes through here on certain days. He never buys water. He says it is bad for the stock.
Sorrel Quist is a lieutenant from Khesh-Ura, here to count the Queen's soldiers. He has counted forty-one. He is not smiling.
The dry well in the inn's cellar is a joke the first owner made. It has not been funny in sixty years.
If the fort falls, I will hang a lantern from the ridge. Not for glory. For the camels. They like a signal.
Vesh-Kar has a wall of spears and a hall of stacked chests. The chests are bait. Do not open them. I mean it. I lost a drover that way.
The fort is quiet. Vesh-Kar's warband has scattered into the dunes, and I am going to sit here and enjoy it.
The first wagon in nineteen days came through at noon. The driver cried. So did the camel. I did not trust myself to look.
A spider-tailed scorpion in the burrow south of the road? The old drovers swear it is real. They also swear the dunes sing.
The beast in the burrow is dead? Then the south stretch of road will be quiet. I will tell the drovers. They will not believe me.
You have a mark that glows, and you saw the Zenith through a window of glass. Whatever you do next, do it before the Queen does.

say: Orla's seal, and Orla's handwriting, and a crate that rattles like a promise. Silver sheeting for the shop, if I am lucky. Signed and stamped.
Take this for the carry, and tell her I said the next one had better not weigh so much.
Vessa Korr. Outfitter. Welcome to the last honest counter before the glass.

Silvered gear, if you can afford it: a full run of blades, staves, bows and maces, with plate, hide, mirage-silk and moonlace to match. Silvering is not magic. It is only very good metalwork with a very good story.
Say what you need; I will name what you can afford. We will meet in the middle and both feel slightly robbed.

lines.text: Silver does not rust, tarnish slowly, and never complains. In that order, it is the perfect employee.
A dagger should weigh what a promise weighs. Enough that you remember it, never so much that you cannot lift it.
I once sold a sword to a man who bought it for the scabbard. He said the sword was a bonus. I respected that.
Hi-potions on the left shelf. Antidotes in the clay jar. Ethers in the blue jar. Nothing in the red jar. Do not ask about the red jar.
Every item here was tested by someone who regretted it, so I trust it.
The Queen's collectors want my stock priced in glass. I price their glass as paperweights.
Plate for a fighter, sized for someone who plans to survive. I charge extra for foresight.
The moonlace robe never warms up. Mages swear by it. Mages also swear at it. Take your pick.
A mirage jacket and a silvered bow. You will vanish from half the dunes and half my profit.
A silvered mace for the devout. It rings when it strikes true. The ringing is free.
The scorpions here shrug off blades and bite through boots. A good hammer or a cold spell will serve better than a good argument.
Tessk sells me scorpion stingers and I sell him jars. We both pretend the transaction is a surprise.
Dilly asked me for a sword. I gave her a broom. She swept the entire shop. I was impressed and slightly threatened.
If you find a glass scale on the road, do not pocket it. It will cut through the pocket and then through you.
Marrak pays me in water. I pay Noor in water. Noor pays Marrak in water. We are a closed economy, and it is rather pleasant.
A rare trader's cart rolled past on the last market day. He did not stop. I do not blame him. My prices are not that bad.
Ellis once offered a map in place of coin. I said I sold gear, not cartography. He sold me the map for a sword. I came out ahead.
I keep a single golden coin in the till. It has never been spent. It is my luck, and my last argument.
Heading for the fort? Buy the antidotes. The scorpions do not play fair, and neither do I, but I charge less.
The fort is down? Then my silver will flow again. I may even lower a price. Do not tell anyone.
A sealed writ in glass? Hold it up to the light. There is writing inside the seal. It is not the Queen's. It is older.
Orc steel on the market this month, with a ridge stamp. I wonder where it came from. I wonder who is asking.
Sandtusk's tusk would make a glorious hilt. Do not tell Kiss'a I said that. She would use it on me.
The road is open and the silver is flowing. You are welcome here any time, provided you pay.

noor_amad.name: Noor Amad
noor_amad.role: keeper of the Dry Well Inn
noor_amad.personality: quiet, shrewd, kind in small deliberate acts
noor_amad.voice: soft-spoken hospitality; compares everything to tea

say: Noor Amad. Welcome to the Dry Well. The well is dry, the beds are not.
Forty coins a night, and mint tea at no charge if you promise to drink it slowly.

lines.text: The first rule of tea: never rush the pour. The second: never rush the guest. The third: never rush the bill.
I serve mint and sage, cardamom and honey. Nobody asks for coffee. Coffee is a rumour out here.
My mother ran the inn before me. She kept a drawer of stranger's letters that never got posted. I kept them. I am still waiting.
The beds are stuffed with desert sage. It keeps the scorpions out and brings strange dreams in.
Guests who snore sleep in the east room. Guests who talk in their sleep sleep in the west. Guests who do both sleep outside.
The Dry Well is named for a joke, a well that holds nothing. Over the years it has held an astonishing number of secrets.
A fighter. I put an extra blanket on your bed. Armour is cold work.
A spell-caster. Do not light the candles with a fingertip. The curtains predate the Queen herself.
A scout, then. Your window faces the road. Your door faces the back. Those are not accidents.
A healer. Please keep a spare vial of antidote under the pillow. Scorpions do not respect locks.
Dilly sleeps in the stable and eats in my kitchen. I have not decided whether to send her a bill or a birthday card.
Old Haggar tells the same eleven stories every night. I know every ending. I still laugh in the right places.
Tessk brews a tea out of scorpion venom and honey. He swears it cures anything. It cures hunger, certainly. Usually permanently.
The rare trader likes my cardamom tea. He pays in coin, and he pays in odd little favours. I keep the favours in a jar.
A traveller left a book of poems under his pillow. I read it every winter. I do not know the author. I know his heart.
After the dimming, nights in the dunes turned colder and days turned hotter. It confused the lizardfolk and delighted the scorpions.
Ellis maps the glass dunes by night. He comes back with sand in every pocket and a smile in every mood.
Sorrel Quist drinks his tea cold and complains it is warm. I have stopped arguing. I serve it cold.
Marrak has not smiled in nineteen days. I put an extra spoon of honey in his cup. It made no difference. I do it anyway.
They say the fort is quiet. The first tea I made after the news tasted different. Better, somehow.
Marrak actually smiled at breakfast. He tried to hide it behind the teacup. He was not successful.
A Khesh-Ura water-writ in your pack? I knew a woman who carried one. She said it opened every door on the road. It did.
I hear the scorpions in the south burrow have gone quiet. A good sign. Or a very bad one, depending on who is listening.
Whatever waits to the east, a bed will be kept for you here. That is not a promise. It is a habit.

tessk_ray.name: Tessk Ray
tessk_ray.voice: field-guide shorthand; classifies everything he sees

lines.text: Dune scorpion: venom, moderate; temper, poor; resistance to frost, none. Observe, then retreat. That is the entire art.
Stonetail scorpions shrug off blades. They hate cold, and they hate lightning. Bring a mage or a long lightning rod.
Lizardfolk are cold-blooded and hate frost more than anything. Fire barely warms them. Ice drops them like stones.
Sand stingers are fast and fragile. A good strike kills one. A poor strike kills the striker's dignity.
Rule one of field work: always read the creature before you strike it. The bestiary in your pack tells you what it weakens to.
I keep forty-one jars of scorpion venom in my tent. Each one is labelled. Eleven of the labels are wrong, and I am too scared to check.
A fighter. Stonetails will blunt your blade, so favour a weapon with an elemental edge, or switch to your skills.
A mage! Bring frost. Bring lightning. Do not bring fire, unless you enjoy being politely ignored.
A scout. Poison tip is wasted on a scorpion, who is rather proud of its own. Switch to a physical shot, or pin and flee.
A healer! May I observe? I have long hoped to watch an antidote work on a living specimen.
Stinger venom, boiled with desert sage, cures a fever. Stinger venom, boiled without sage, causes a slightly different fever.
The Spidertail is a rumour, and a very specific one. Scorpion body, spider spinnerets, and a tail that drips both venoms. I have a drawing. It is mostly guesswork.
I once caught a scorpion with my bare hands. It was the proudest day of my life and the longest week of my recovery.
Vessa buys my stingers by the dozen and sells them as charms. I do not mind. I only mind that she sells them for more.
Dilly asked if she could learn herb lore. I told her to start by learning which herbs bite. She nodded and wrote it down.
In the glass dunes, the scorpions are clear. Beautiful, and vicious. You can see their hearts. Please do not tell Marrak I went there.
The lizardfolk shamans heal their friends, and that is the reason to fell the shamans first. A healer left standing can undo a good ten minutes.
Ellis maps, I classify. We have a very civilized argument about whether the dunes are alive. I say yes. He says only on weekends.
Vesh-Kar is a lizardfolk, and a large one. Ice will bite him, fire will not. And do not fight him in the open: his warband will crowd you.
The warlord is down! I would love a sample of his scales. Preferably intact. Preferably while he is not looking.
The hybrid is real? I will need to redraw three diagrams and apologize to my wife. Both in the same afternoon.
You felled a boar as big as a wagon? A boar! No venom, no sting, nothing to study. What a waste of a good hunt.
A creature that exploits your weak points is a danger. A creature that exploits your assumptions is a teacher.
Watch what a creature resists, and you will learn what it fears. That is the first and last lesson of every field guide.

dilly_prout.name: Dilly Prout
dilly_prout.voice: run-on excitement, running metaphors, and names for every camel

lines.text: I run letters to Khesh-Ura and back, three days each way! I have run the road eighty-four times and only been chased by scorpions twice.
The trick to running in the dunes is to run on the ridges, not the troughs. The ridges are firm and the troughs are sand soup.
I name all the camels. Biscuit, Duchess, Sir Reginald, and one who is just called No. He knows why.
Marrak says I will wear out my boots before I wear out my legs. I say good. I have three more pairs.
I saw a warband march along the ridge last week. They looked like green beads on a string. Very pretty. Very scary.
My plan for later: caravan guard, or mapmaker, or both. I am flexible.
Is that sword genuine? May I hold it a bit? I will only drop it in sand.
Do you do real magic? Can you make a little flame in my hand? Not hot! Just a little! I want to feel it!
You look like a runner! Do you run in the dunes? Do you run on the ridges? I have so many questions!
A priest! Can you bless my boots? They are very important boots.
Tessk says every scorpion has a weakness. I asked if I had one. He said, 'Yes, you ask too many questions.'
Noor gives me tea with honey when I come back from a long run. It is the best moment of any week.
Old Haggar spins tales of the Queen in her youth. He says she used to be nice. I do not believe him. Nobody is nice with a sword.
A coin turned up on the road, stamped with a sun and a crown. I suspect it is haunted, so it lives in my sock.
Ellis let me draw one line on his map. It is the coast. Well, it is a wiggly line, but it is MY wiggly line.
The dunes sing sometimes. Low and sad, like a camel humming. Tessk says it is wind. I say it is the dunes being lonely.
Once a peddler with a canary-coloured wagon gave me a sweet whose flavour belonged to somewhere I have never visited. I miss it anyway.
Vessa let me polish a silvered dagger. I saw my face in it. I look very brave. I looked more brave than the dagger.
The fort north of here flies a green banner. When the wind drops, you can hear drums from three miles away. I run faster then.
The banner is DOWN! I saw it from the ridge! I ran the whole way back! My legs have forgotten how to stop!
Marrak gave me a medal! It is a bottle cap on a string, but it is a MEDAL! I am never taking it off!
Do you really have a glowing hand? Can I see? Does it hurt? Does it itch? Does it glow when you sneeze?
Tessk told me about the Spidertail. A scorpion with spider legs. I stopped sleeping for two nights. Tessk says that is a good sign.
I am going to run all the way to the sea one day. Will you tell me about it when you get there? Please?

old_haggar.name: Old Haggar
old_haggar.personality: gruff, nostalgic, a born exaggerator with a soft heart
old_haggar.voice: war-story rhythms, 'back in my day', and an unreliable body count

lines.text: I guarded caravans for forty years and lost eleven fingers. I count them in my sleep, and they never add up.
Back in my day the road was safe, and the Queen was a girl with a quick smile and a very bad sword.
I once fought nine scorpions with a bent spoon. I was younger. They were smaller. The spoon was sturdier.
Marrak thinks I tell too many stories. I think Marrak tells too few. Between us we are an average of boredom.
The first rule of caravan guarding: never be the first, never be the last. Be the one in the middle, slightly ahead.
I fought beside a wizard once. He turned a scorpion into a teapot. We drank from it for a week. Best tea I ever had.
A fighter. You hold your blade like a man who has been taught well and corrected rarely. Good. Stay that way.
A mage. In my day, mages wore pointed hats and apologised for them. You have the right posture.
A scout. You walk like my first partner. He died laughing, which is the way he would have wanted it.
A healer. Good. My knees have an opinion about the stairs, and I would like a second opinion.
I remember when Ismerel was only a magistrate. She used to ask for water and say thank you. Now she asks for the sun and does not.
The glass dunes were sand once. Then one night they were not. I saw it happen from the ridge. A light, a hum, and silence.
I carried a tax-collector's sack once across the Scorch Road. It weighed more coming back. I did not ask why.
Dilly reminds me of my youngest. Fast, loud and fond of danger. I give her my best advice. She ignores every word.
A rare trader gave me a little charm once. It stopped one bad day from happening. I never found out which.
Noor keeps a bottle of old brandy behind the kettle. She thinks I do not know. I have known for nine years.
I counted forty-one Queen's soldiers in the last month. Forty-one. In my day a Queen needed four, and a bad temper.
Tessk says every creature has a weak spot. I say so does every man. Mine is soup.
Vesh-Kar was a decent soldier once. He served my old captain. Then the Queen found him and gave him a banner. Banners ruin good soldiers.
The warlord is down? Good. Though I will say, I pity the man a little. He only did what he was told. That is the oldest sin there is.
They put up a lantern on the ridge tonight. First in nineteen days. I wept. Do not repeat that to Marrak.
I heard you killed a troll at Khesh-Ura's water gate. At your age I fought a troll with a ladle. It won.
The Scorch Road is a long road, and the Queen made it longer. But a road ends where a traveller stops. Do not stop.
Hask, was it? I remember a Hask. He sold me a rope once. It broke. I broke his nose. We were both satisfied.

ellis_vane.name: Ellis Vane
ellis_vane.personality: dreamy, meticulous, obsessive about the colour of sand
ellis_vane.voice: map legends, compass bearings, and wistful asides about places he has not seen

lines.text: A good map lies about distances but never about direction. A bad map lies about both. A great map lies about what it is for.
The glass dunes shift every night. I redraw them every morning. I have a shoebox full of drawings that were right for one day only.
The Scorch Road runs east for forty miles, then bends toward the Queen's labyrinth. Nobody has drawn the last ten miles and returned.
Sand is not one colour. It is red at dawn, gold at noon, violet at dusk, and the exact shade of regret at night.
I sketch with charcoal because ink bleeds in the heat. Charcoal forgets nothing and forgives everything.
I have mapped nine towns, seven roads, forty wells and one lie. The lie is the most popular.
A fighter. I always draw fighters in the margin, with a little sword. It reassures the reader.
A mage. The old star-charts show every bright point as a doorway. I have often hoped to step through one.
A scout. Show me your sketch of the road, and I will point out which parts you invented. Everyone invents the middle.
A healer. I have a blister the shape of the Hollow Sea. It is a very good map. It is also very sore.
The old priests placed their wells along a straight line. Every priest's well lines up with the sunset on a certain day. I have not worked out which.
Where the glass dunes begin, the compass needle spins. Not wildly. Slowly, patiently, like a dancer waiting for music.
I have a map of the Queen's labyrinth, drawn from rumour. It has seven walls, a thousand turns, and one very large X. I am told the X is a minotaur.
Dilly helped me measure the ridges once. She ran them barefoot and shouted the distances back. It was remarkably accurate.
Noor's inn is on every road map I own. It is the only place a traveller can be sure of finding on a bad day.
The stars here move faster than anywhere else. I am convinced of it. My assistant says it is the wine.
Haggar claims he walked to the sea once. There is no sea within five hundred miles. I drew it in anyway. For his sake.
A rare trader once bought a map of my footprints. He said they were more honest than the roads. I thought that was lovely.
The Toll Fort stands on a ridge with a sheer drop on three sides. It has one road in and one road out. Choose your moment well.
I saw the banner fall through my glass. It looked like a green leaf in autumn. I drew it, in green.
The road east is open. I will sketch it as far as the bend, and then I will wait for someone brave to describe the rest.
I have redrawn the Boar Hollow from your description. Did it truly have a ring of wallows? I hope so. It is a lovely detail.
The Sand Warren is on my map, in pencil. I can erase it now, or leave it as a ghost. I prefer ghosts.
If you reach the labyrinth, send word. I will leave a blank page in my atlas. Fill it in, when you are able.

sorrel_quist.name: Lieutenant Sorrel Quist
sorrel_quist.role: Khesh-Ura patrol officer on observation duty
sorrel_quist.personality: stiff, dutiful, secretly anxious about every decision
sorrel_quist.voice: report-style sentences; ends statements with 'for the record'

lines.text: Lieutenant Sorrel Quist, Khesh-Ura patrol, here to observe and report. I observe a great deal and report very little. For the record.
I have counted forty-one of the Queen's soldiers on this road in the past month. That is nine more than the last count and thirty-six more than I would like.
Orders: do not engage, do not be seen, do not be late. I am batting a hundred percent on the second. For the record.
The Toll Fort has a garrison of sixty lizardfolk and fourteen scorpion handlers. The handlers terrify me more than the garrison.
I have written four reports this week. The first three were returned for being too cheerful. For the record, I am not cheerful.
Marrak offers me tea. I decline. Noor offers me tea. I decline. Dilly offers me tea. I accept. She is the only one who pours it hot.
A fighter. The Khesh-Ura guard would take you. The pay is poor, the hours are worse, and the uniform itches. For the record.
A mage. Please keep your spells outside the camp. The last wizard in the patrol turned my report into a flock of birds. For the record.
A scout. You are a splendid observer, I assume. Please observe quietly. Please observe somewhere else. For the record.
A healer. My sergeant has a cough. He claims it is nothing. He also claims the sky is not blue. For the record.
The Queen's soldiers wear glass pins on their collars. Each pin is a splinter of the Zenith. I would like to know how she gets so many.
Old Haggar tells me the Queen used to be a magistrate. I have checked. She was a magistrate. Then a treasurer. Then a Queen. The paperwork is suspiciously smooth.
Ellis maps the dunes. I verify the maps. We disagree on the position of every landmark. It is a cordial relationship.
A rare trader passes through at intervals. I have noted it. I have no jurisdiction to question him. For the record.
Szazz writes to me weekly asking for news of the water. My reply is the same each week: wait. I would like to reply with something new.
I have been in the dunes for fifty-one days and counted every tent in this camp. There are eleven. There were ten yesterday. I have not found the eleventh owner.
Tessk showed me a drawing of a scorpion with a spider's tail. I filed it under 'hysteria'. For the record.
The camels in this camp are better-behaved than my recruits. I would swap, if the Guard allowed it. It does not. For the record.
The Toll Fort is held by Vesh-Kar. I have submitted a request for reinforcements. The reply is expected in the next season. For the record.
The fort has fallen. I would like to say I predicted it. For the record, I predicted a different outcome entirely.
My report on the Toll Fort has been accepted. It was my first without a correction. I am telling everyone. For the record.
The water gate at Khesh-Ura is open again, I hear. Szazz wrote to me in a handwriting I have never seen. Joyful. For the record.
A rare trader's cart was in camp this morning. I did not buy anything. I did, however, write a very detailed report about the cart.
Whatever you do next, I will record it, and I will record it kindly. That is the one thing a report can do. For the record.
